person.name: Charles_Rennie_Mackintosh
person.summary: Charles Rennie Mackintosh was a Scottish architect and designer whose buildings, interiors, furniture, and decorative work shaped the Glasgow Style. He designed the Glasgow School of Art and the Willow Tearooms while working in Glasgow, then spent his final years painting watercolors in France.

conclusion: Glasgow School of Art continues to be studied by architects and designers. The Willow Tearooms and surviving interiors preserve Mackintosh’s designs for rooms, furniture, lighting, and decoration. Museums including the Hunterian in Glasgow hold and exhibit his watercolors of Port-Vendres and Roussillon.

events.title: Born into a Glasgow Police Family
events.description: William McIntosh served as superintendent and chief clerk of the City of Glasgow Police in Townhead, Glasgow. Charles Rennie Mackintosh was the fourth of William and Margaret Mackintosh’s eleven children and their second son.

events.title: Studies at Allan Glen's
events.description: In 1880, Charles Rennie Mackintosh began attending Reid's Public School and Allan Glen's Institution in Glasgow. He remained at these schools through 1883.

events.title: Begins Architectural Apprenticeship
events.description: In 1884, Charles Rennie Mackintosh began an architectural apprenticeship with John Hutchinson in Glasgow. He attended evening classes at the Glasgow School of Art. Practical office work accompanied his formal study.

events.title: Joins Honeyman and Keppie
events.description: In 1889, Charles Rennie Mackintosh joined Honeyman and Keppie in Glasgow as a draughtsman and designer. The firm was a major architectural practice in the city.

events.date_note: The group formed around 1892 and exhibited together by 1894
events.title: Forms the Glasgow Four
events.description: Around 1892, Charles Rennie Mackintosh met Margaret Macdonald, Frances Macdonald, and James Herbert MacNair at the Glasgow School of Art. Francis Henry Newbery introduced the artists after seeing similarities in their work. They began working together as The Four.

images.caption: The Immortals, Glasgow artists’ group including the Glasgow Four
images.creator: Unknown authorUnknown author

events.background:
Margaret and Frances Macdonald came to the Glasgow School of Art as day students. Mackintosh and MacNair attended evening classes while training in architecture. By 1894, the four were placing work together in student exhibitions. Some of the exhibited pieces were collaborative.

Their early work received a mixed response. The Macdonald sisters used gaunt, linear figures that showed the influence of Aubrey Beardsley. Critics called the imagery “ghoulish.” The local nickname “The Spook School” attached to the group before “The Four” became its familiar name.

Much of the group’s collaborative work during the 1890s centered on the two sisters. Their Hope Street studio, opened in 1896, produced illustrations, embroidery, gesso panels, leaded glass, and repoussé metalwork. The four artists’ related approaches contributed to the Glasgow Style.

events.title: Wins Art School Commission
events.description: In 1896, Honeyman and Keppie won the competition for a new Glasgow School of Art building. Charles Rennie Mackintosh served as project architect. He designed the building and its interiors, furniture, and ironwork.

images.caption: Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh Building east façade
images.creator: Ad Meskens

events.background:
Francis Henry Newbery prepared the brief from his experience running the school and from Department of Science and Art requirements. He supported Mackintosh’s proposal with the school governors and government advisers. Mackintosh had been the practice’s lead designer since 1892. During the 1890s, Keppie had come to leave much of the firm’s design work to him.

Construction of the school at 167 Renfrew Street ran from 1897 to 1909. The completed project helped establish Mackintosh’s international reputation.

events.title: Marries Margaret Macdonald
events.description: On 22 August 1900, Charles Rennie Mackintosh married Margaret Macdonald, an artist and designer, in Glasgow. They established their first home in Glasgow and worked together on decorative and interior designs.

events.title: Becomes a Firm Partner
events.description: In 1901, Charles Rennie Mackintosh became a partner in Honeyman, Keppie and Mackintosh. He had become the practice’s lead designer after joining it as a draughtsman and designer.

events.title: Designs Vienna Music Room
events.description: In 1902, Fritz Waerndorfer commissioned Charles Rennie Mackintosh to furnish the music salon of his villa in Vienna. Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh designed its wall panels, including The Seven Princesses, a work based on Maurice Maeterlinck’s play of the same name.

images.caption: The Seven Princesses frieze for the Warndorfer music salon
images.creator: Margaret MacDonald

events.title: Completes Willow Tearooms
events.description: In 1903, Charles Rennie Mackintosh completed the Willow Tearooms in Glasgow for Catherine Cranston. He designed its facade, rooms, and furnishings, including the [[Room de Luxe]]. Margaret Macdonald contributed decorative work to the interiors.

images.caption: Miss Cranston’s Willow Tearooms, designed by Mackintosh
images.creator: photographer J.C. Annan

Room de Luxe.explanation: The Willow Tearooms’ most elaborate room, designed as an especially refined interior for women patrons.

events.title: Leaves the Partnership
events.description: In 1913, Charles Rennie Mackintosh resigned from Honeyman, Keppie and Mackintosh as the Glasgow architectural practice declined in profitability. He attempted to establish an independent architectural practice in Glasgow.

events.title: Moves to Walberswick
events.description: In 1914, Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh left Glasgow for Walberswick, a Suffolk village. Mackintosh made watercolor landscapes and flower studies there.

events.title: Arrested as Spy Suspect
events.description: During the First World War, Charles Rennie Mackintosh was suspected of being a German spy and was briefly arrested in Walberswick. He and Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh were living in the Suffolk village at the time.

events.title: Settles at Port Vendres
events.description: In 1923, Charles and Margaret Mackintosh left Walberswick and settled in Port-Vendres on the Mediterranean coast of southern France. They sought a warmer climate and lower living costs. Charles painted the harbor and the Roussillon landscape in watercolors.

images.caption: Port Vendres, France, watercolor by Charles Rennie Mackintosh
images.creator: kitmasterbloke

events.background:
By 1923, Mackintosh had entirely abandoned architecture and design. His watercolors examined the relationship between built structures and the natural landscape. The work produced a large portfolio of architectural and landscape paintings.

The Mackintoshes remained in France for two years. Illness eventually forced their return to London.

events.title: Death in London
events.description: A lump in Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s tongue brought him from Port-Vendres to London for treatment in 1927. Jessie Newbery arranged surgery at Westminster Hospital, and Randolph and Birdie Schwabe gave him a home in Hampstead while he recovered. Margaret Morris tried to strengthen his impaired voice and teach him sign language. After a relapse, Desmond Chapman-Huston gave the Mackintoshes a home in Bayswater. Mackintosh died in a London nursing home on 10 December 1928.
